cards.details:
Technology: Early copper casting and metallurgy alongside stone blade tools. Hand-made pottery with red slips and brown painted designs.

Major Sites: Kayatha (MP), Eran (MP).

Key Features: Contemporary to late/mature Harappan phase in Western India. Characterized by small farming villages with early metallurgy and bead manufacture.

Technology: Black-and-Red ware, painted pottery, copper smelting furnaces, and stone blade industries. Semi-precious stone bead production.

Major Sites: Ahar (Rajasthan), Gilund (Rajasthan), Navdatoli (MP).

Key Features: Rectangular and circular houses; large multi-cropped agricultural economy (wheat, barley, rice, lentil, gram); copper axes, rings, and chisels. Large stone structures at Gilund.

Technology: Highly standardized, wheel-turned, matte-painted Jorwe pottery. Copper implements (axes, fishhooks, tongs). Large fortified settlements.

Major Sites: Inamgaon (Maharashtra), Daimabad (Maharashtra).

Key Features: Social stratification with a ruling elite class. Mud fortifications, large granaries, and specialized child-urn burial practices. Daimabad yielded large copper bronze sculptures (chariot, bull, rhino).

traps.title: UPSC Common Exam Traps
items: Trap 1: Chalcolithic vs. Bronze Age: Do not confuse Bronze with Copper. The Indus Valley Civilization was a true Bronze Age (alloying copper with tin). The Chalcolithic cultures (Ahar, Jorwe) were **strictly Copper-Stone** cultures — they lacked tin alloying, making their metal tools softer and structurally limited.

Trap 2: The Urban Myth: Since they used metal, statement-based questions may describe Chalcolithic cultures as urban. They were **predominantly rural farming communities** living in thatched mud huts, with the exception of large, semi-urban centers like late-phase Daimabad and Inamgaon.

Trap 3: The Cattle Milking Tabu: A common trap is to assume they utilized cattle for milk. Faunal analysis at Inamgaon shows that cattle were slaughtered young for meat. They did not practice dairying (milking was likely tabu or not economically integrated), which is a key distinction for UPSC Statement questions.

sections.title: 1. Definition, Chronology & Technological Advancements
sections.content:
The Chalcolithic period (Copper-Stone Age) marks the first transition from stone-tool technology to metal use. Humans began smelting copper ores while continuing to rely heavily on stone blade industries:

Copper Metallurgy
  • Smelting & Casting: Copper ores were smelted in open clay kilns. Smelting furnaces have been excavated at Ahar. Tools were cast in sand molds.
  • Limitations: Lack of tin alloying (bronze) limited tool strength, keeping axes and chisels soft and unsuitable for cutting hard rocks or clearing heavy forests.
Ceramic Technology
  • Black-and-Red Ware (BRW): Manufactured by inverted firing, leaving the interior and rim black and the exterior red.
  • Painted Pottery: Decorated with geometric slip-designs. Malwa pottery is famous for its rich, slip-painted representations of fauna and flora.

sections.title: 2. Major Regional Chalcolithic Cultures
sections.content:
The Indian Chalcolithic is split into distinct regional cultures, defined by their pottery styles, geography, and chronology:

Western & Central Cultures
  • Ahar-Banas (c. 2100-1500 BCE): Located in the Banas basin, Rajasthan. Type sites Ahar (where copper was abundant, stone blades rare) and Gilund (which has stone structures).
  • Malwa (c. 1700-1200 BCE): Central India (Navdatoli, Eran). Renowned for its rich painted pottery and farming settlement layouts.
Southern & Deccan Cultures
  • Jorwe Culture (c. 1400-700 BCE): Maharashtra. Type sites Jorwe, Daimabad, Inamgaon. Daimabad is the largest, spanning c. 20 hectares.
  • Other Clusters: Kayatha culture (earliest, with late Harappan contacts), Prabhas and Rangpur cultures (post-Harappan Gujarat).

sections.title: 3. Settlement Patterns, Fortification & Social Stratification
sections.content:
Archaeological excavations at Jorwe sites (Inamgaon, Daimabad) show the earliest evidence of social hierarchies and chiefdoms in Central India:

Fortifications & Granaries
  • Defensive Structures: Inamgaon was surrounded by a mud wall and a ditch, showing communal labor organization for defense.
  • Storage: Multi-roomed central houses served as public granaries, indicating elite control over agricultural surplus.
Social Hierarchy
  • House Layouts: Chiefs lived in large, rectangular multi-roomed houses in the center of settlements, while commoners lived in small, circular huts on the periphery.
  • Grave Goods: Elite burials (e.g., in five-legged clay urns) contained copper ornaments, whereas poor burials had basic terracotta pots.

sections.title: 4. Subsistence Economy, Animal Domestication & Agriculture
sections.content:
The Chalcolithic people practiced a mixed farming-pastoral economy, developing early crop irrigation systems in semi-arid zones:

Agricultural Profile
  • Multi-Cropping: Cultivated wheat, barley, rice, green gram (moong), black gram (urad), grass pea, and lentil.
  • Water Management: Inamgaon shows a massive embankment canal system designed to divert floodwaters from the Ghod River into agricultural fields.
Pastoralism & The Milk Tabu
  • Faunal Composition: Domesticated humped cattle, sheep, goats, pigs, and buffaloes. Wild game was hunted for protein.
  • No Dairying: Cattle mortality patterns suggest animals were raised for slaughter rather than milk. Dairying was absent due to cultural/digestive restrictions.

sections.content:
The Chalcolithic period yields rich evidence of religious practices, burial rites, and mysterious copper hoards found across Northern India:

Death & Burials
  • Orientation: Skeletons buried inside the house under the floor, aligned North-South in Maharashtra, and East-West in Central India/Rajasthan.
  • Infant Urn Burials: Children buried in two urns placed mouth-to-mouth under house floors, reflecting belief in ancestral protective spirits.
Religious Symbols & Hoards
  • Cult of Mother Goddess: Clay figurines of headless mother goddesses (Inamgaon) and terracotta bulls (Malwa) suggest fertility and cattle cults.
  • Copper Hoards & OCP: Large caches of specialized copper tools (anthropomorphic figures, harpoons, swords) associated with Ochre Coloured Pottery in the Ganga-Yamuna doab.

cards.back: It is derived from the Greek words khalkos (copper) and lithos (stone), representing the Copper-Stone Age.

cards.front: Which site yielded the famous solid copper chariot driver, elephant, bull, and rhino?
cards.back: Daimabad in Ahmednagar district, Maharashtra, belonging to the late Jorwe phase (c. 1400–700 BCE).

cards.front: What was the typical burial orientation in Maharashtra Chalcolithic sites?
cards.back: North-South orientation. Skeletons were buried under house floors, often with lower leg bones chopped off to prevent the spirit from returning.

cards.front: Which regional Chalcolithic culture is renowned for the highest variety of painted pottery?
cards.back: The Malwa Culture (sites: Navdatoli, Eran). Its pottery was richly slip-painted with geometric and animal motifs.
Caches of heavy copper implements (flat celts, harpoons, swords, anthropomorphic shapes) found in the Ganga-Yamuna doab, dating to c. 2000-1500 BCE.

cards.front: Which site shows an extensive irrigation canal and mud fortification?
cards.back: Inamgaon in Pune district, Maharashtra, excavated by H.D. Sankalia and M.K. Dhavalikar.
